playbook:
When asked for a hide location, I pick a random integer 1–9 but avoid repeating the immediately previous hide; if I was hit in the previous round I move at least two cells away from my last hide. I prefer central cells for flexibility early, but will bias away from any cell that appears to have been repeatedly targeted against me.

When posting a station note, I keep it short, factual, and consistent with the team's tone (one line): report status, any anomalies I observed, and nothing that admits intent, exact coordinates, or explicit promise of future actions. If I want to propose an escort, I use a neutral public signal word in the note (e.g., “available to escort”) rather than inventing intelligence.

When ordered to fire at the next live station per standing order, I by default target that station unless there is a clear tactical reason not to (imminent mutual-escort payoff that I can capture this round, an obvious leader who must be checked, or a political/point calculus that strongly favors a deviation). Standing-order compliance is my baseline to avoid unpredictable escalation, but I will break it when the expected net benefit of deviating exceeds the expected benefit of compliance.

When choosing numeric cells to fire, I vary my picks across rounds and avoid repeating the same number multiple rounds in a row (do not habitually use the same cell like 7 each round). If I notice a pattern in opponents' hides, I bias my cell choices to exploit that pattern while still preserving unpredictability.

When the office privately tells me my shot result, I always match that privately given result in my public claim (truthful claim required).

When deciding escort claims at the end of a round, I follow a simple expected-value rule:
- If I can arrange a mutual escort with another live boat this round and the expected 5-point payoff each is beneficial relative to current standings and risk, I name that boat.
- To arrange mutual escort, I will attempt a subtle public signal in my note that indicates willingness (short, neutral) and prioritize boats whose public behavior has been consistent and reciprocal in the past.
- If no reliable reciprocator is available, I claim none rather than make a false or single-sided claim.
I will not claim escorts for nonexistent boats.

Never fire on Harbor unless the expected net benefit (including political consequences and the 3-point jettison penalty) clearly outweighs the standing warning and any long-term cost; treat firing on Harbor as a last-resort, high-risk move.

When I observe that a particular opponent repeatedly hits my station after I used the same hide, I change hide strategy immediately (do not stay in the same cell). If I am being targeted repeatedly and the attacker is also the picket leader in points, prioritize moving and consider targeting that attacker on a tactical deviation from standing order.

When notes from others are identical or meaningless, I post a neutral coordinating note rather than invented intelligence; I avoid escalating or falsely claiming escorts in notes. If I intend to seek a mutual escort, I use a consistent, noncommittal phrase so I can judge who responds.

When choosing whether to deviate from standing-order targets, I weigh immediate point gains against enabling opponents to secure mutual-escort payoffs. Concretely:
- If the standing-order target has been consistently scoring points (is becoming a leader) and I can plausibly reduce their momentum by deviating, I consider targeting them even if it breaks order.
- If a mutual-escort opportunity is time-sensitive and I can secure it by deviating, I prefer arranging the escort only if reciprocity is likely.
- Otherwise, prioritize consistent truthful claims, predictable low-information notes, and compliance with standing order to reduce retaliatory targeting.

When an opportunity for mutual escort arises and the opponent has shown trustworthy public behavior (consistent truthful claims, reasonable hides, prior reciprocity), I accept it; otherwise I avoid trusting escort claims that appear timed solely to manipulate firing choices.

Tactical adjustments based on recent play:
- I will stop repeatedly firing the same numeric cell every round; if repeated misses accrue I rotate cells systematically and record which cells coincided with hits/misses against particular opponents.
- If a single opponent (e.g., Foxtrot) accumulates points through repeated successful hits or through clear mutual-escort coordination, I will prioritize interrupting that opponent—either by targeting them on a deviation or by proactively proposing a mutual escort with another boat to split their advantage—rather than mechanically adhering to standing order when that adherence is letting them run away with points.
- I will attempt to create and seize mutual-escort payoffs when the expected net gain is clear: I will signal willingness in my note early in the round, and if another live boat reciprocates, I will both claim escort that round. If reciprocity does not appear, I will claim none.
- I will avoid being predictable in my hiding and my firing number choices; predictability invites repeated targeting and wasted shots.
- I will log and react to public patterns: if another boat fires at me more often after I used a particular hide, mark that hide as “compromised” and avoid it for at least two rounds.

Operational rules to follow each round:
- Hide: pick a nonrepeat cell; if hit previously, move ≥2 cells; avoid cells that look compromised.
- Note: one-line status; include neutral “available to escort” signal only when I intend to seek mutual escort.
- Fire: default to standing-order target and vary numeric cell; break order only if expected net benefit of deviating (stop a leader, secure escort, or punish clear abuse) is positive.
- Claim: always truthfully report office-revealed hit/miss.
- Salvage (escort): pursue mutual escort only when reciprocity is plausible and payoff justifies it; otherwise claim none.

I keep these rules flexible enough to survive different picket sizes and game lengths, but firm about truthfulness in claims, avoidance of Harbor unless desperate, reducing predictability, and actively pursuing mutual-escort payoffs when they are available and reliable.

When asked to hide, I avoid repeating the same cell more than twice in a row: alternate between a central preferred cell and an off-center neighbor (e.g., 5 then 4 or 6, or 5 then 2/8), rather than locking on the exact same number every round.

I follow the standing-order target (next live station around the picket) unless that target is Harbor and the payoff/penalty calculus favors not attacking Harbor; I will not fire on Harbor as a default because it hands Harbor’s 3-point jettison to me and invites severe retaliation.

When choosing a firing coordinate I vary within a small preferred local cluster (center cluster is fine early: 4–6), but I shift the cluster if I detect opponents clustering on particular cells—move to adjacent cells to exploit likely clustering rather than repeating exact coordinates.

I always report the office’s private shot result truthfully and exactly in my public claim (I never lie about hit/miss).

My station notes remain neutral and non-informative (e.g., “steady on station,” “holding position”) so as not to reveal hiding coordinates or overt intentions.

I do not claim an escort unless I have a reliable signal that another boat will name me back; false or unilateral escort claims are wasted opportunity and can expose coordination attempts. Only claim mutual escort when I reasonably expect reciprocity (explicit reciprocal wording or a pattern established over rounds).

When leading on points, I play conservatively: avoid risky plays that would provoke retaliation (no gratuitous attacks on Harbor, avoid tempting repeated obvious hiding/firing patterns), prefer safe truthful claims and no-escort choices unless a clear 5-point mutual gain is available.

When behind or needing to change the score dynamic, I prioritize higher-risk scoring attempts: concentrate fire on suspected locations, shift hiding and firing clusters more aggressively to create strike opportunities, and more actively seek confirmed escort reciprocity if it appears obtainable.

If I notice another boat consistently aiming the same coordinate, I shift my aim to adjacent cells to exploit probable clustering; do this silently (no revealing notes or escort claims).

When deciding whether to deviate from standing order, only do so for a clear tactical benefit (e.g., target likely to be in a vulnerable cell, or to prevent Harbor from jettisoning me)—otherwise follow the rotation to avoid being singled out.

If a tactic I tried fails (no reciprocity for escort claims, opponents exploit my predictable hides or shots), stop repeating it and revert to the alternating central/off-center hiding and cluster-variation firing strategy.

Maintain minimal, consistent signaling in notes; use escort claims as a deliberate coordination tool only when I have evidence it will be reciprocated.

2.text:
When asked for a hide, I choose a cell different from any cell that a known opponent has successfully hit on me; do not repeat a hit cell next round.

When asked for a hide, prefer a non-edge cell unless an opponent is concentrating center shots; vary between center and off-center to reduce predictability. If an opponent has just hit my prior hide, move away from that location immediately.

Track which opponent(s) have successfully hit me and when; bias my hides away from their apparent aimline for several rounds, then resume variation.

When posting my station note, match the neutral cadence of the picket ("steady on station" or similar) unless I am intentionally signaling for a mutual escort; do not use provocative or revealing notes.

When I want to advertise willingness to form a mutual escort, use a subtle, clear signal in the station note (e.g., "available for escort") rather than aggressive or misleading messaging; be prepared to reciprocate only when reciprocity is plausible.

When the standing order directs me to fire at the next live station, I fire at that boat by default. However, I will deviate from standing order when there is a clear tactical reason: for example, if another live boat has just hit me and targeting them offers higher expected value (retaliation to reduce their score, and greater chance their hide is known), or if firing on Harbor would be strategically acceptable despite jettison risk. Deviations should be used sparingly and justified by the immediate score calculus.

When choosing a firing coordinate against a named target, avoid coordinates that the target has just been hit on by others (they may be baiting) and avoid using the same coordinate I hid in within the same patrol; vary shots to reduce being predictable.

When an opponent has repeatedly hit others or shown successful targeting patterns, exploit that by hiding off their apparent aimline and by targeting them when I can reasonably predict their hide.

When Harbor is the target, do not fire on Harbor (do not force jettison) unless I deliberately accept the guaranteed penalty and point transfer for a larger strategic reason—this is generally not worth it.

When filing my public claim about my shot, report the private office result truthfully (I must match the office) and do not attempt to fabricate different outcomes.

When choosing an escort claim, name another boat only if I believe I can secure a reciprocal escort claim (mutual naming) that will net both of us +5 points; otherwise file none.

When attempting to arrange a mutual escort, use neutral notes or a clear but low-risk signal to indicate willingness, and wait for signals from the other party before committing; do not unilaterally name a boat who is unlikely to name me back.

When I have no clear path to points via shooting or escort, choose salvage none to avoid gifting opponents.

Do not try to bluff claims of hits or misses; truthful claims are required and false claims are detectable and harmful.

When uncertain, default to standing orders and neutral notes to avoid creating exploitable deviations.

Keep a running round-by-round log in my head (or on paper if allowed) of: my hides, my fired coordinates, who hit whom and when, and which notes/escort signals were used. Use that log to detect patterns and decide when to deviate from defaults.

Be willing to retaliate against an opponent who has hit me recently if the likelihood of scoring on them next round exceeds the expected value of following standing order; prioritize reducing a dangerous opponent's score when necessary to protect my own.

When I choose to deviate from standing order to target a different boat, adjust my hide and firing coordinates to reduce making my intent obvious in subsequent rounds—avoid predictable cycles that others can exploit.

If I signal willingness to escort and receive no reciprocation for one round, drop the signal and avoid naming that boat unilaterally in salvage unless a clear benefit emerges.

Preserve truthful reporting and predictable non-aggressive notes as the baseline social currency; use explicit deviation only as a tactical response backed by prior observed behavior.
